narrative:
Your application was denied because the prediction estimated an 84.1% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That is a high estimated risk, so the admissions decision treated your application as too risky to approve.

The strongest reason was your class standing in your third year: you were in the lowest decile, while accepted students averaged around the middle of their class. This was the single most influential factor and pushed the prediction toward failure. Your first-year class standing was the second most important factor, and it also pushed toward failure for the same reason: you were in the lowest decile, compared with accepted students who averaged near the middle. Your undergraduate GPA was the third most important factor, but it worked in your favor: at 3.30 it was slightly above the accepted-student average of 3.23 and pushed toward passing. It was not enough to offset the much stronger concern about your law-school class standing.

To move forward, ask admissions whether there is an appeal or reconsideration process, and request specific conditions for admission. Meet with an academic advisor to understand why your class standing was low and build a concrete improvement plan. Consider bar-exam preparation early, additional rigorous coursework, and, if feasible, retaking the LSAT; your score of 35 was below the accepted average of 37.18. Then reapply with evidence that your academic trajectory and exam readiness have improved.
